# Black Friday Website Crash: What to Do in the First Hour If Your Store Goes Down
Black Friday falls on 27 November 2026 and Cyber Monday on 30 November.  A crash at 09:00 on sale day is a bad time to find out that nobody has the hosting login or the ad account password.
## Worked scenario (illustrative)
A WooCommerce store selling outdoor gear sends its main Black Friday email at 08:00. By 08:06 product pages take 20 seconds to load and checkout returns 502 errors. The agency's external monitor confirms failures from two regions, and the host's status page is clear, so the problem is on the store's side.
## At a glance
- Confirm the outage from outside your own network and from more than one location before you change anything.
- Return 503 with a short maintenance page during the outage. Google treats 503 as temporary; a 200 error page can show up as a soft 404 in Search Console.
- Cut demand first: pause ads and scheduled email sends, switch off expensive features, and queue visitors if your CDN plan supports it.
- Stripe retries undelivered webhooks for up to three days in live mode and PayPal resends IPN messages for up to four days, so most "paid but no order" cases can be recovered after the site comes back.
- After recovery, compare payments with orders for the outage window before you announce that everything is fine.
## Why it matters now
- Google's guidance on planned downtime recommends a 503 status, with an optional Retry-After header that Googlebot may use to decide when to recrawl. The same guidance warns about sites that return 200 for downtime pages.
- Cloudflare Waiting Room, which holds excess visitors in a queue, is available on Business and Enterprise plans only and requires the hostname to be proxied through Cloudflare.

seltz.title: Holiday Traffic Surges Put E-Commerce Site Reliability to the Test
seltz.snippet:
As the holiday shopping season kicks into high gear, a recent Network Solutions industry survey and research report looked the pressure that e-commerce merchants are under during the peak of the retail season—in particular, Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

Researchers at the e-commerce solution provider identified issues that sites face when traffic suddenly spikes. They found that site reliability is a genuine bottom-line issue rather than just a technicality for retailers and brands.

The report’s authors said that technical failures on higher-traffic shopping days go beyond the customer just staring at an error screen. Abandoned carts due to slow pages or payment gateway timeouts are a major factor in customers simply switching their allegiance to a competitor.

Unexpected site downtime or poor performance during a major shopping event results in immediate money loss and long-term damage to a retailer’s reputation. When thousands of shoppers are all wanting to buy from a merchant at the same time, business owners will quickly hit the limits of their server infrastructure, database connection limits and checkout process.

The report revealed that of those businesses surveyed, 61 percent said they experienced a website failure or serious slowdown during a sale or traffic surge in the past year, while 32 percent reported a payment or checkout failure that prevented orders during a sale or traffic surge.

Among those respondents whose sites had failed, 72 percent said high traffic or hosting limits as the cause, while 36 percent said it took more than an hour to restore full functionality.
